prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B041 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The first round sharpened the case rather than weakening it. Six members now converge on one topological story, and all six credit Kane and Molenkamp, so the remaining dispute is narrow. The discovery has a theoretical origin (the Kane-Mele Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal) and a decisive laboratory fingerprint (quantised edge conductance in HgTe wells). It has more than fifteen years of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES and scanning probes, and it has changed how materials are searched for and designed. The committee aims to name the topic and the people responsible for the original work, and I think a citation tied to the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification identifies that chain more precisely than one stretched to three-dimensional materials. As an experimentalist in electron microscopy I weigh the existence of a clean, reproducible experimental signature heavily, and this case has one.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state that Molenkamp observed, and Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy are central to the three-dimensional theory; none can be named in a three-person configuration. Hasan's ARPES work is a real experimental pillar that my configuration omits, and the citation must be worded narrowly enough not to imply that the 3D phase is being credited. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions is a smaller worry than I first thought, but it will be raised in public. Finally, B013 has a cleaner credit, and I have not heard an argument that makes topological insulators the lesser science, only that they are the harder allocation.

responses.point: Danielsson holds Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan and argues that the experimental side deserves two slots, otherwise the 3D phase that made topological insulators a materials class has no credited experimentalist.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument for a different trio and I have reconsidered it carefully, but I do not move. The first observation of the topological state in HgTe is the discovery that turned the Z2 theory into physics, and Mele is a joint originator of that theory. Taking him out while keeping Kane splits a single paper-level contribution, which sits badly with the idea that the prize names those responsible for the original work. The 3D case also rests on a theory chain (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Roy) that we cannot credit in full, so adding Hasan alone would be less tidy than it looks. I agree the Mele-versus-Hasan choice is a judgment about attribution, not about merit, and I would keep Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan as the fallback if the committee decides experimental breadth outweighs theoretical continuity.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B013 first, regards B041 as scientifically convincing but less ready on credit, and says Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state and cannot be credited.
responses.response: The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang point is the fairest statement of the problem and I do not claim to resolve it. I disagree that it makes B041 less ready, though. The prize has regularly honoured a three-person subset of a larger community, and the test is whether the named people are defensibly central, which Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are. Zhang's death also removes him from consideration. The committee should be candid in its deliberation that the HgTe theory credit is incomplete, and the citation should describe the quantum spin Hall effect broadly enough that it does not claim priority over that prediction. I accept that B013 needs no such compromise, and that is why I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll rates B013 as a clean invention with a measured 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, and says he would not oppose B041 if conceptual reorganisation is judged to outweigh instrumental invention.
responses.response: On the chair's question about which criterion should decide, I weigh conceptual reorganisation and an experimental fingerprint together, and B041 has both. I take his point that the lattice clock is a physical insight about the magic wavelength and not a refinement, and I think a narrow citation would answer the 2005 and 2012 adjacency. My reservation is not about worth. It is that the redefinition of the second, which he rightly says should not carry the argument, has not yet happened, while the topological case is already settled. If the committee can honour only one of the two this year, I would still choose B041, and I would not block B013 in a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, would make the case for a second prize part rather than displace Mele for 3D work, and flags that the 2016 prize covers part of the conceptual background.
responses.response: I agree with his approach and with the idea that a second part for the 3D materials is the cleaner way to recognise Hasan than displacing Mele. I would not take that route this year because the opening support is concentrated in one topological entry and the second part would force a three-person cut across two quantum-materials stories, with its own attribution dispute. On the 2016 question, the earlier prize recognised topological phase transitions and the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz framework, not the spin-orbit-driven insulator class or any material realisation. The Z2 classification and the HgTe observation are new relative to it.

uncertainties: Whether Mele or Hasan should hold the third slot remains a judgment call, and I hold the Mele version with moderate confidence.
How far a citation can acknowledge the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Moore-Balents contributions without naming them or overstating priority.
Whether the committee reads the 2016 prize as covering topological matter more fully than I do.
I rely on memory for the priority chronology and have not verified it against sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B041, B013 or B014. My connections are Chalmers colleagues (including fellow committee member Johansson), David Clarke at IBM, Japanese academic exchanges and the international microscopy federation, and none involves Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Katori or Ye as far as the profile shows. This is unchanged from round 1.
